scenes.tts: Dead bacteria changed living bacteria into the dead donor's type. What crossed between them? Living rough cells usually lacked a capsule and were generally harmless. Heat-killed smooth cells could not grow. Yet mixing them sometimes produced living, capsule-bearing cells of the donor type. Their descendants kept that type. Neither ingredient alone produced that outcome.

scenes.visual: COLOR MAP for the whole film: DNA blue, protein gold, living rough recipients teal, donor-type capsule green. Hook first on one full-frame schematic bench: teal rough cells move in from the left; heat-killed green-halo donor cells fade but remain visible above. The groups combine, a large question mark appears, and living green-halo descendants divide below. Mark the bacteria picture 'schematic'. Keep the cells drifting or dividing while narration continues.

scenes.visual: Transform the central question mark into the title 'What Followed the Trait?' for two seconds. Keep one teal rough cell and one green-halo descendant large behind the title, then return them to the same bench positions.

scenes.tts: Griffith's mouse experiment revealed transformation, a heritable change in bacterial type. It did not name the substance responsible. But it pointed to an assay. Later laboratories moved it into culture. Add a donor extract to rough recipients, then count colonies with the donor capsule. The active material could now be followed through purification. A scored phenotype replaced guesswork.

scenes.visual: On the carried bench, first show a small schematic mouse icon beside the cells, then fade it while a label 'later laboratories: culture' appears. Only then shrink the donor cells into a labelled 'donor extract' drop. The drop flows through successive purification funnels while a fixed recipient tray fills with teal colonies. Green capsule halos appear only around transformed colonies; a counter rises beside them. Preserve the same tray and positions throughout.

scenes.tts: Researchers purified the active fraction, then challenged separate samples with enzymes. Protein-digesting enzymes left transformation active. An RNA-digesting enzyme also left it active. Each enzyme was first checked against a known target. Now predict the decisive test. If intact DNA is required, what should happen after a DNA-depolymerizing treatment?

scenes.visual: Split the same active-fraction stream into three large gates labelled 'protein', 'RNA' and 'DNA'. The protein and RNA branches feed recipient trays whose green transformation lamps stay on. The DNA branch stops before its tray. Show a small checked target chip beside each enzyme gate. End with the DNA gate and question filling most of the frame.

scenes.visual: Hold the question 'If intact DNA is required, what happens here?' above the DNA-depolymerizing gate for 4.5 seconds. Let blue DNA-labelled blocks drift slowly toward the gate while the transformation lamp remains neutral, not yet revealed.

scenes.tts: The DNA-depolymerizing preparations removed activity. Chemistry also matched nucleic acid, and transformed cells passed the donor type through generations. Avery, MacLeod and McCarty concluded that the fraction was principally, if not solely, DNA. Their methods could not exclude a protein below detection. The hedge preserved the experiment's detection limit.

scenes.visual: Blue DNA blocks fragment as they cross the DNA gate, and the recipient tray's transformation lamp drops to off. Transform the three gates into an evidence ledger with 'chemistry', 'selective destruction' and 'heredity' as three moving rows. A very small gold question-mark chip stays below a labelled detection line; do not label it as actual protein.

scenes.tts: One system was not enough. Hershey and Chase turned to phage T two, a virus of E coli built from a protein coat around DNA. They marked sulfur-containing protein with one tracer and phosphorus-rich DNA mostly with another. The film keeps protein gold and DNA blue. Where each color travelled could separate their roles. This was an independent physical test.

scenes.visual: Slide the bacterial assay left and transform its blue DNA and gold uncertainty colors into two large schematic phage cartoons. Each phage is a gold coat surrounding a blue labelled block, never a molecular structure. One tracer badge locks to gold protein and a different badge locks mostly to blue DNA. Both phage drift toward a large teal bacterium.

scenes.tts: Both phage batches attached to bacteria. Blending removed material still outside, and centrifugation separated cells from fluid. Most gold sulfur moved into the fluid. Much less blue phosphorus did. The stripped cells still produced phage, and progeny carried far more parental phosphorus than sulfur. Exact percentages are on screen.

scenes.visual: Keep the teal bacterium central. Gold coats attach outside while blue blocks move inward. A blender vortex shears external gold material away, then the frame becomes one fixed centrifuge tube with fluid above and a cell pellet below. Animate gold and blue counters into the correct compartments. Show exact lesson values only on screen: fluid sulfur about 75%, fluid phosphorus about 15%; progeny sulfur less than 1%, phosphorus 30% or more. Progeny phage bud into a fixed tray at right.

scenes.tts: The tracers set limits. Sulfur could not report sulfur-free material, so the experiment did not show that no protein entered. Some sulfur stayed cell-associated. That distinction matters. The result was narrower: most DNA entered, and most coat stayed out. Inheritance travelled mainly with the DNA label.

scenes.visual: On the same tube, place a translucent 'unmeasured sulfur-free material?' bracket outside the gold tracer legend. Keep a small gold remainder by the pellet instead of clearing it. Then widen the blue path from attached phage through the pellet to progeny, while the gold path mostly bends into fluid. Use 'most' labels, never 'only' or 'none'.

scenes.tts: Across two independent systems, heritable change followed DNA. Transformation required intact DNA in a purified fraction. Phage reproduction followed the DNA-rich tracer into cells and progeny. Neither experiment claimed more than it measured. Convergence, not one perfect experiment, carried the argument. Together, they made DNA the strongest candidate for inherited information in these systems.

Gold protein paths remain visible but do not meet the card. Slowly pulse the two independent blue routes while the bounded label 'these systems' settles below.
